edition.locus: Vossius 1684 Opera omnia (archive bub_gb_DY2xvRwPetMC), Latin column, chapter VI, printed pp. 45-46 (PDF pages 69-70)

source_text:
Consequens vero mihi videtur, ut quod est simplex, etiam sit immortale. Et quo pacto illud, ausculta: Nihil eorum quae sunt, seipsum corrumpit; alioquin enim ne initio quidem constitisset. Quae autem corrumpuntur, ex contrariis corrumpuntur. Nam omne quod corrumpitur, dissolvitur: quod dissolvitur, compositum est: at compositum, multarum est partium: quod ex partibus constat, ex iis scilicet constat differentibus: quod vero differens est; idem non est: Quamobrem cum simplex sit Anima, neque ex pluribus partibus constet; quia nec composita est, nec dissolvi potest: sequitur eam incorruptibilem, et immortalem esse.

Praeterea, quidquid alieno cietur motu, nec ex se ipso, sed ex eo, a quo movetur, vivendi habet facultatem; illud tam diu permanet, quod ab illa intrinsecus operante vi conservatur: at ubi ea cessaverit, et ipsum quod ab ea movebatur, desinat necesse est. Quare cum Anima a seipsa moveatur, nunquam esse desinit. Haec enim ita se consequuntur, ut quod a seipso movetur, semper moveatur, quod semper movetur, nunquam deficit: quod nunquam deficit, fine caret: quod finis est expers, non corrumpitur: quod non corrumpitur, est immortale. Ergo si Anima a se ipsa movetur, ut superius demonstratum est; erit igitur ex vi iam propositae ratiocinationis, incorruptibilis et immortalis.

Praeterea, quodcunque a proprio malo non corrumpitur, corrumpi non potest: malum autem bono contrarium est; ideo et illius corrumpendi vim habet. Non enim aliud est corporis malum, quam passio, morbus, et mors; sicut e contra virtus eius est, pulchritudo, vita, sanitas, et firma constitutio. Si igitur Anima a suo malo non corrumpitur; malum autem Animae, est metus, intemperantia, invidia, et similia: quae tamen omnia vivendi ac movendi facultatem ipsi non auferunt: Anima ergo est immortalis.
orientation: Three arguments show that the soul is immortal: what is simple cannot be dissolved, what moves itself never stops moving, and the soul's own evils do not take away its life.
pass_a_gloss: It seems to me consequent (consequens) that what is simple is also immortal (immortale). And in what way, listen (ausculta): none of the things that are destroys (corrumpit) itself; for otherwise it would not even have stood (constitisset) at the beginning (initio). But things that are destroyed are destroyed from contraries (ex contrariis). For everything that is destroyed is dissolved (dissolvitur); what is dissolved is composite; but the composite is of many parts; what consists of parts consists, namely (scilicet), of differing (differentibus) ones; but what is differing is not the same (idem). Wherefore, since the soul is simple and does not consist of several parts, because it is neither composite nor can be dissolved, it follows that it is incorruptible (incorruptibilem) and immortal. Besides, whatever is stirred (cietur) by another's motion (alieno motu), and has the faculty of living (vivendi facultatem) not from itself but from that by which it is moved, that remains (permanet) so long as it is preserved (conservatur) by that power (vi) operating within (intrinsecus operante); but when that has ceased (cessaverit), the very thing that was moved by it must also cease (desinat). Therefore, since the soul is moved by itself (a seipsa), it never ceases to be. For these things so follow one another (se consequuntur): what is moved by itself is always moved; what is always moved never fails (deficit); what never fails lacks an end (fine caret); what is without end (finis expers) is not destroyed; what is not destroyed is immortal. Therefore if the soul is moved by itself, as was demonstrated above, it will then be, by the force (vi) of the reasoning (ratiocinationis) now set forth, incorruptible and immortal. Besides, whatever is not destroyed by its own evil (proprio malo) cannot be destroyed. But evil is contrary to good (bono); therefore it also has the power (vim) of destroying it. For the evil of the body is nothing other than suffering (passio), disease (morbus) and death (mors), just as on the contrary its virtue (virtus) is beauty (pulchritudo), life, health (sanitas) and firm constitution (firma constitutio). If therefore the soul is not destroyed by its own evil; and the evil of the soul is fear (metus), intemperance (intemperantia), envy (invidia) and similar things, which all nevertheless do not take away (auferunt) from it the faculty of living and moving (vivendi ac movendi facultatem): the soul therefore is immortal.

choices.why: One English word through the chain of argument.
Print reads 'quod' where 'quoad' is the expected sense; kept as printed.
The body's proper goodness, not moral virtue.

pass_b_english: It seems to me to follow that what is simple is also immortal. Listen to how this is so. Nothing that exists destroys itself; otherwise it would not have existed even in the beginning. Things that are destroyed are destroyed by contraries. For everything that is destroyed is dissolved; what is dissolved is composite; what is composite has many parts; what consists of parts consists, of course, of parts that differ; and what differs is not the same. Since, then, the soul is simple and does not consist of many parts, because it is neither composite nor able to be dissolved, it follows that it is indestructible and immortal.

Moreover, whatever is set in motion by another's movement, and has its power of living not from itself but from what moves it, lasts as long as it is kept in being by that power working within it; when that power ceases, the thing it was moving must also cease. So, since the soul is moved by itself, it never ceases to be. For these things follow one from another in this way: what is moved by itself is always moved; what is always moved never fails; what never fails has no end; what has no end is not destroyed; what is not destroyed is immortal. If, then, the soul is moved by itself, as was shown above, it will be, by the force of the reasoning just set out, indestructible and immortal.

Again, whatever is not destroyed by its own evil cannot be destroyed. Evil is contrary to good, and so it has the power to destroy it. For the evil of the body is nothing other than suffering, disease and death, just as, on the other side, its excellence is beauty, life, health and a sound constitution. If, then, the soul is not destroyed by its own evil, and the evil of the soul is fear, intemperance, envy and the like, none of which takes from it the power of living and moving, then the soul is immortal.
notes: Edition chapter VI ('An immortalis nostra sit Anima').
'corrumpo' rendered 'destroy' and 'incorruptibilis' 'indestructible' throughout, so the chain of argument keeps one word.

Doubtful reading: 'illud tam diu permanet, quod ab illa ... vi conservatur' (printed 'quod' where 'quoad' is the expected sense) rendered 'lasts as long as it is kept in being by that power' (print 'quod' confirmed on the page image, PDF p. 69).
'virtus' of the body rendered 'excellence' (its proper goodness), not moral virtue.
'ut superius demonstratum est' kept as printed, though the earlier chapters show the soul moving the body rather than stating in so many words that it moves itself.
The self-motion argument follows Plato, Phaedrus 245c-e, and the 'own evil' argument Plato, Republic 10.608e-610e; philosophical sources, not Scripture, so nothing is cited in the text.
The final argument's 'if' clause runs into its conclusion as printed; the English keeps one sentence.
